headline: OpenAI's Astra solved 10 decades-old math problems for $2,000 in compute cost
summary: OpenAI's unreleased Astra model generated fully machine-verified proofs for ten open math problems, some unsolved for up to 48 years, at an inference cost of just $2,000.
details: On August 1, 2026, OpenAI announced that its internal model, Astra, produced machine-verified proofs for ten open problems in mathematics and theoretical computer science. Several of these problems had remained unsolved for decades, with some dating back 48 years. The total inference cost for these breakthroughs was approximately $2,000.

OpenAI substantiated its claims by publishing a 249-page manuscript and the underlying Lean 4 proof certificates on GitHub under an Apache 2.0 license. Lean is a proof assistant that rigorously checks every logical step by machine, ensuring no unverified steps are accepted. The repository shows a zero "sorry" count across all ten results, confirming the internal consistency of every formalized proof step.

This achievement reframes the cost conversation in mathematical research. It highlights that an AI model, capable of searching proof space at machine speed and verified by Lean, can transform a multi-year human research program into an overnight, three-figure compute bill. The ratio of decades of expert human effort against $2,000 of inference cost is the most significant takeaway.

Fields Medalist Timothy Gowers reacted positively to the news, though he cautioned that the results are still being digested by the mathematical community. Thomas Bloom, curator of erdosproblems.com, called the ten results "big news" on X, ranking them above earlier AI math achievements. However, it's important to note that none of these ten proofs have yet undergone formal peer review.

This is not an isolated incident, following GPT-5.6 Sol's work on a 50-year-old math conjecture in July and an earlier unit-distance counterexample in May 2026. Frontier AI labs are increasingly using formalized mathematics, with its unforgeable pass/fail signals from proof checkers, as a clean way to demonstrate a model's capacity for original research, beyond just retrieving existing knowledge.

The next steps involve whether any of these ten proofs will survive full peer review unchanged, and if Astra can replicate this success on problems chosen by outside mathematicians. A single overnight run serves as a powerful demonstration, but a consistent track record on adversarially chosen problems will provide stronger evidence of its capabilities.

headline_marked: [[Nvidia reportedly halts GeForce RTX 5090 production]] in favor of AI data center and professional GPUs
headline: Nvidia reportedly halts GeForce RTX 5090 production in favor of AI data center and professional GPUs
summary: Nvidia is reportedly redirecting its GB202 processors to more lucrative data center and professional GPUs, potentially making the RTX 5080 24GB the new top-tier consumer card.
details: Nvidia has reportedly ceased selling its GB202 graphics processors for consumer-grade GeForce RTX 5090-series add-in-boards. This unverified claim, cited by leakers @hongxing2020 and @Zed__Wang, suggests the GB202 silicon will now be exclusively for data center and professional graphics cards.

A leaked factory notice indicates that no more RTX 5090 models, including D variants for China, will be manufactured. The highest-end GeForce card would then be the RTX 5080 24GB, with the 16GB version discontinued.

While unofficial, this alleged decision makes economic sense for Nvidia. The company can sell GB202 processors in data center and professional cards at substantially higher prices than consumer GeForce RTX 5090s.

For instance, the RTX Pro 5500 shares the RTX 5090's 21,760 CUDA cores but offers 84GB GDDR7 memory, targeting lucrative professional visualization and AI applications. The fully-fledged RTX 6000 Pro with 24,064 CUDA cores and 96GB memory can sell for $15,000.

By discontinuing GB202-based GeForce products, Nvidia could prevent its consumer cards from competing with its own professional accelerators in the AI sector. This redirects limited manufacturing to higher-margin products without sacrificing gaming market position, as neither the RTX 5080 nor 5090 have direct rivals.

Even if shipments halt, RTX 5090 boards won't vanish instantly due to existing inventory at partners, distributors, and retailers. However, a lack of new GB202 supply will inevitably lead to declining availability and affect prices.

Nvidia may also be preparing to refresh its RTX 50-series lineup. Rumors suggest GeForce RTX 50 Super cards, including an RTX 5080 Super with 24GB GDDR7, were postponed but could now be revived. The RTX 5080 24GB would benefit from better memory supply without the RTX 5090.

With next-gen Rubin-based RTX 60-series GPUs rumored for late 2027 or 2028, this discontinuation could leave a significant gap in the enthusiast gaming market. Those seeking the absolute best graphics card might need to act soon.
